<reason>Both sides executed at a high level and followed format cleanly (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure). Side B's strongest route was the "safe or useful, pick one" trap, which forced Side A to commit to pseudonymized individual histories inside a secure room with aggregate-only outputs. But Side A's answer is the mainstream, plausible model for sensitive-data research (census/hospital/tax precedents grounded in ordinary knowledge), and Side B's rebuttal that "noise-checked aggregates are too coarse to answer cascade questions" was asserted rather than demonstrated — counterfactual simulations and rate comparisons can plausibly be computed inside with aggregate outputs. Meanwhile, Side A's "proves too much" argument — if session data is too dangerous for vetted, logged, penalized researchers, it is far too dangerous to leave solely with ad-targeting teams and secret briefings — was never squarely neutralized; Side B's auditor distinction (sanction vs. study) honestly answered the pressure question but conceded that individual-level viewing under legal duty is feasible, weakening the "impossible to make safe" framing. Side B's whitewash worry was answered by the mandate-plus-logging design, and the authoritarian-reciprocity point remained speculative against Side A's point that coercion exists regardless. Side B's layer-resolution of the exposure/whitewash "contradiction" was clever and memorable, keeping this competitive, but Side A controlled the decisive comparison: independent replication versus trust-me accountability.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's pressure Q1 forcing Side A to pick a data level, followed by Side A's A1 commitment to pseudonymized histories computed inside a secure room with aggregates out — and Side B's closing exploitation ("every safeguard kills the finding; every finding kills the safeguard"). Sharp exchange, but Side A's secure-computation answer and "proves too much" cross-application (auditors and ad teams already see this data) held the ground.</best_rebuttal>
